models.quote: GPT-6 Astra verdict: for what I use it for I like it and will likely keep using it. However, it did need a few more AGENTS[.]md tricks to keep it on track.

history.quote: Opus 4.5 is good enough to let me finally do side projects where I know precisely what I want but not necessarily how to implement it.

I was paying for both Claude Code and Codex, but Opus 4.7 is a pain to work with due to shrinking session limits and GPT 5.5 is surprisingly more reliable for what I am doing with better session limits.
GPT-5.6 Sol is indeed a great model that does live up to the hype, and I’ve had to create new projects just to have an excuse to test its limits.

review_style.value: Luna subagents re-check until all satisfied; he watches benchmark diffs
review_style.quote: After you are done making changes, before handing off to the user, spin up the subagents again to confirm your implementation matches their hypotheses and ask for potential further areas of improvement. Keep iterating until ALL subagents are satisfied with your implementation.

also.quote: It’s easy to see if an algo gamed the benchmarks if you see the benchmark file in the git diff—agents can’t cheat that (easily, anyways).
That said, it’s more hands-off than I’d like and there’s a lot of explicit faith that the newer agents aren’t just really good at cheating the benchmarks in ways I cannot detect.
Once the work is completed and manually reviewed, I manually commit the work to git, with the message referencing the specific prompt file so I have good internal tracking.

harness.value: Zed Agent, long Markdown prompt files, prompts queued overnight
harness.quote: The Ur-Prompt, combined with the rules and constraints in my AGENTS.md + the two breakthroughmaxxing prompts + a competition prompt pass + a refactor prompt pass with GPT-6 Astra allows me to just queue the prompts overnight, go to bed, and wake up to superfast software.

history.value: Terminal Claude Code, prompt files tagged in, manual commits
history.quote: My approach to prompting is to write the potentially-very-large individual prompt in its own Markdown file (which can be tracked in git), then tag the agent with that prompt and tell it to implement that Markdown file.

parallelism.quote: To best accomplish innovative implementations, you **MUST** spin up 7-12 independent distinct "subagents" by running a long-duration CLI command (do not use the subagent tool) which can explore and evaluate different feasible hypotheses for improving the performance, usability, and security of this crate.

rules_files.value: AGENTS.md for Rust (245 lines) and for Python, shared as gists, ALL-CAPS rules
rules_files.quote: If the code is not fully optimized before handing off to the user, you will be fined $100. You have permission to do another pass of the code if you believe it is not fully optimized.

signature.caption: 7–12 cheap critics per pass
